lines.text: 3.3 The Components We Need in Tiny Amounts
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are the components we eat by the spoonful.
There is another set that we need in amounts so small they are measured in
milligrams — and yet a person who goes without them falls seriously ill.
The strongest way to see what these components do is to look at what happens
when they are missing. Read the two cases below and work out the answer
yourself before reading on.
Q CASE
Case 1 — The sailors' disease
On long sea voyages in earlier centuries, sailors fell ill in a particular way.
Their gums swelled and bled, their teeth loosened, old wounds reopened,
and many died — often months from any battle or storm.
In 1746, during a voyage, the Scottish physician James Lind made a
careful observation. Sailors who were given lemons and oranges recovered.
Sailors who were not, did not.
The condition is called scurvy.
Now interpret Case 1. Lind's sailors were not short of food — ships carried
salted meat and dry biscuit in quantity. They were short of something present
in lemons and oranges and absent from salted rneat.
That something is now called Vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of Vitamin C
in the diet, and it is prevented and cured by foods that contain it — citrus fruits
like lemon and orange, and also amla, guava and green chilli.
Notice how much Lind's method matters. He did not guess. He compared two
groups of sailors who differed in one respect, and drew a conclusion from the
difference. That is an experiment, conducted at sea in 1746, and it saved a
great many lives.
THINK-SPOT
Lind's sailors ate plenty of food and still fell ill.
What does that tell you about the difference between
eating enough and eating well?
